db976f0b505d: 100+ properties sounds like a project. It is a wizard, three questions, and a live preview that shows you the calendar before you save anything.
4893ef85e18a: Most Salesforce components with real depth make you learn them twice: once to understand the properties, once to remember which combination you picked last time. The Setup Wizard exists so you do neither. It asks what you are scheduling, writes the configuration as metadata, and hands you a name you can use anywhere.
80a1e6a60a29: Two ways in, plus two shortcuts
a5581499a679: The Create New tab opens on two paths. Two more tabs sit beside it for configs you already have.
e3e1bdd6e4d0: Three questions about what you are scheduling. Best for first-time setup.
91227bae6390: Every property visible, with a live preview. Best when you know exactly what you want.
379d62fca719: Your saved configs with their component type. Open one to edit or clone it.
b29d9a8e3dce: Paste a config from the Config Library or another org.
eb76cbd6cce8: Two paths on Create New. Most admins start on the left.
b6294e42b3c1: A whole booking config, start to finish. Every object and field is picked from a filtered dropdown; nobody types an API name.
f58374224588: The config name and which component it is for: Dates, Dates & Times or Resource Booking.
d1cd2ee08581: The object that holds the records, the date field, the parent lookup, and the resource if you book one.
b3f3113c28c8: Start and end time, slot interval and business hours, for configs that capture times.
2813d2c0dc15: Status colors, hover fields and edit mode.
d3ca15ebd1cc: A summary of every choice, then save.
ebfe55ad6771: The three questions that decide everything
226905d10a1d: The guided path asks about the <t1>shape</t1> of the records you want, rather than about properties. Every answer combination is valid, and together they decide what the component writes:
e776e80d2dcf: <t1>Do you need times, or just dates?</t1> Dates alone, a time on each date, or a parent block with sub-blocks for the gaps inside it.
77356e6140f3: <t1>Are you booking a resource?</t1> None, one at a time, or several at once.
94b8c704a402: <t1>Should consecutive dates collapse into a range?</t1> One record per date, or one record with a start and an end.
86123e18c57a: The answers are independent, so they describe the whole grid of possibilities rather than a menu of presets. Monday through Friday for six weeks can be thirty records or six. You choose that here, on purpose, before any data exists.
5e914e82bbce: Each answer card carries a small diagram of the records that choice produces.
62cd5a5c78e9: A live preview, before anything is saved
5d6fee259ab4: The preview pane renders a working calendar underneath the form as you change properties. Turn on two-month view and it appears. Add status colors and the cells fill. It is the actual component, so what you approve is what you deploy.
b890dd5b47b4: The expensive mistakes in scheduling configuration are shape decisions you cannot see until real records exist. Seeing the calendar respond while you are still deciding removes most of that risk.
85f07b93ced9: The preview is the real component. What you see is what deploys.
b6f825ee8bca: Inside the steps: Object & Fields, Time Fields, Status & Display
4c5024665f0e: Every field is a dropdown, filtered to the object you picked and to the field types that fit.
16d917a49e53: Two steps do most of the heavy lifting on a booking or scheduling config. Time Fields maps the start time, end time and interval your calendar needs. Status & Display is where the visual polish lives, from status-driven cell colors to which fields show on hover.
70212de20603: Time Fields: time fields, interval and business hours.
9e657dba6f98: Status & Display: colors, hover fields and edit mode.
9e1060a48a12: On Status & Display, pick a status field, map a color to each value, and choose whether the color paints the calendar cell, the time slot grid, or both. Add hover fields so pointing at a booking previews the details.
6ef1b91add49: Saving deploys a Custom Metadata record. Three things follow:
76f3f8569399: <t1>It is deployable.</t1> Custom Metadata moves through your normal release pipeline, sandbox to production, like any other component.
63a06b08012d: <t1>It is reusable.</t1> Put the name in <t2>Config Name</t2> on any component and it picks up the whole configuration. One config, many placements.
9b6997413616: <t1>It stays in your org.</t1> Nothing is stored on a vendor server, so the configuration is yours and it is visible in Setup.
93a44bd7e810: <t1>About the deploy.</t1> Custom Metadata deploys are asynchronous. The wizard waits about two minutes and then, if the record has not appeared, shows you the deploy id and a link to Setup → Deployment Status. A busy org can take longer than the wizard waits, and the deploy still finishes.
8783c0f0371c: <t1>Who can run it.</t1> Assign <t2>MultiDatePick - Setup</t2> to admins who build configs. It includes the Setup Wizard. Everyone who uses the calendars gets <t3>MultiDatePick - User</t3>, and <t4>MultiDatePick - All Access</t4> covers both.
3ed427a37e1b: Import, export, and the mapping step people miss
d2f3c9231fbb: The Import tab takes a JSON configuration and turns it into a saved config. That is how the <t1>Config Library</t1> works: 40+ ready-made configurations covering time-off requests, room booking, hot-desking, interview scheduling, fleet reservation and more.
052365d2aeba: From the Config Library to a working Lightning page: copy, paste, deploy, drop the component on the page and give it the config name.
0037fffacb83: The step that saves the most time is <t1>Smart Field Mapping</t1>. Library configs reference the demo objects; your org has its own. The wizard scans every reference the moment you paste, flags each one your org does not have, and puts a dropdown next to it sourced live from the object's real field list. Remap in the wizard, click Apply, and it deploys with the rewritten JSON. No text editor, no hunt and replace, no re-uploads.
abf0dfc34cd1: Each unresolved reference gets a dropdown from your org's schema.
c4a4b826f608: Paste a config, remap, save. No XML, no CLI.
08e5d77cab36: Export works the same way in reverse, which makes configurations shareable. A config that works in one org is a paste away from working in another.
63b7a1e97dee: Using the config once it exists
f9b64daaf35a: Drop any of the three components onto a Lightning record page, app page, Home page or Experience Cloud site, set <t1>Config Name</t1> to the name you chose, and leave every other property blank. The config supplies them. On App, Home and Experience pages, put the parent record in <t2>Static Parent Record Id</t2>.
42d801046e61: The same applies inside a Screen Flow: put the config's name in <t1>Config Name</t1> and every on/off setting comes from the config. You do not set a single checkbox in Flow Builder; the few flow-only ones (Required, Show Inline, Output Date Ranges as JSON) are off unless you turn them on. Pass the parent record into <t2>Parent Record Id</t2>.
